## Soursop and Cancer: What the Evidence Shows

**Conclusion: The claim that soursop "cures cancer in humans" is not supported by scientific evidence.** No clinical trials in humans have demonstrated that soursop treats or cures cancer.

**What the evidence actually shows:**

Laboratory (in vitro) and some animal studies have found that compounds in soursop—particularly acetogenins like annonacin—can kill cancer cells in a petri dish or reduce tumor growth in animal models. This has led to widespread promotion of soursop/graviola as a "natural cancer cure" online. However, fact-checking organizations and medical institutions are consistent on this point: laboratory findings have never been replicated in human clinical trials. As PolitiFact notes, "there haven't been human studies, so we don't know whether it can work as a cancer treatment or not" (https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/). Africa Check similarly found no evidence supporting claims that soursop leaf tea cures cancer (https://africacheck.org/fact-checks/meta-programme-fact-checks/no-evidence-soursop-leaf-tea-cures-cancer-depression).

Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, a leading cancer research institution, acknowledges soursop contains biologically active compounds but does not endorse it as a cancer treatment, and Wikipedia notes both MSK and Cancer Research UK state that "cancer treatment using soursop is not supported by reliable clinical evidence" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop).

**Important safety concern:** Annonacin, the same compound touted for anticancer activity, is a mitochondrial toxin linked to neurotoxicity and an atypical form of Parkinson's disease, particularly documented in populations with high soursop consumption in Guadeloupe (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14521988/).

**Bottom line:** Soursop shows lab-based anticancer potential worth further study, but no rigorous clinical trials confirm it "cures" cancer in humans, and it carries potential neurotoxic risks. Relying on it instead of proven treatments would be medically unsound.
